title: The Emin Pasha Relief Expedition
intro: Henry Morton Stanley led a force of nearly 700 men to relieve Emin Pasha, the besieged Egyptian governor of Equatoria. Instead of the shorter route inland from the east coast, the expedition went by sea round the Cape to the mouth of the Congo, up the river and through the Ituri rainforest to Lake Albert.
ending: The expedition reached Bagamoyo on the east coast on 4 December, with Emin and the survivors of the march. Stanley was at first acclaimed, but criticism followed as the deaths of so many of its members and reports of brutality became known.

legs.title: By sea round Africa to the Congo

stops.text: Stanley arrived from London. Egyptian objections to the Congo route were overridden by a telegram from Lord Salisbury, and the expedition was permitted to march under the Egyptian flag.
stops.quote: Stanley departed London on 21 January 1887 and arrived in Cairo on 27 January. Egyptian objections to the Congo route were overridden by a telegram from Lord Salisbury, and the expedition was permitted to march under the Egyptian flag.

stops.text: Stanley arrived after leaving Cairo on 3 February. He persuaded the Sultan to grant a concession and made two agreements with Tippu Tib, one naming him Governor of Stanley Falls, much criticised in Europe as a deal with a slave-trader, and one for carriers.
stops.quote: Stanley left Cairo on 3 February, joined up with expedition members during stops in Suez and Aden, and arrived in Zanzibar on 22 February.

stops.text: The expedition left Zanzibar on 25 February and rounded the Cape of Good Hope on its way to the mouth of the Congo.
stops.quote: The expedition left Zanzibar on 25 February and, rounding the Cape of Good Hope, arrived at Banana at the mouth of the Congo on 18 March.

stops.wp: Banana, Democratic Republic of the Congo
stops.text: The expedition arrived at the mouth of the Congo somewhat unexpectedly, because a telegraph cable had broken and local officials had received no instructions.
stops.quote: Their arrival was somewhat unexpected, because a telegraph cable had broken and local officials had received no instructions.

stops.text: Chartered steamers brought the expedition to Matadi. There the carriers took over and brought some 800 loads of stores and ammunition overland, slowly, in the height of the rainy season and with food short.
stops.quote: Chartered steamers brought the expedition to Matadi, where the carriers took over, bringing some 800 loads of stores and ammunition to Leopoldville on the Stanley Pool.

stops.text: Of the river steamers King Leopold had promised, only one worked. Stanley requisitioned two from missionaries, overriding their protests, left many stores behind, and announced a rear column and an Advance Column.
stops.quote: On 21 April, the expedition arrived at Leopoldville. King Leopold had promised a flotilla of river steamers, but only one worked: the Stanley.

legs.title: Up the Congo and through the Ituri forest

stops.text: The voyage up the Congo began on 1 May. At Yambuya on the Aruwimi the villagers refused permission to stay, so Stanley attacked and drove them away and made the village a fortified camp. He left for Lake Albert on 28 June.
stops.quote: The inhabitants of Yambuya refused permission to reside in their village, so Stanley attacked and drove the villagers away, turning the deserted village into a fortified camp.

stops.text: The expedition looked down on the lake on 13 December, with 169 of the 389 who left Yambuya still alive, and built Fort Bodo at Ibwiri on the plateau above. In April 1888 Emin brought his steamer to the south end of the lake and met Stanley there.
stops.quote: Emin brought his steamer to the south end of the lake, and met Stanley there on the 29th, who was surprised to find the figure of Emin to have "not a trace on it of ill-health or anxiety"

legs.title: The search for the rear column and the way out

stops.text: Stanley left the lake on 24 May and Fort Bodo on 16 June in search of the rear column. At Banalya he found Bonny and a handful of starving carriers. Barttelot had been shot in a dispute and Jameson had gone down to Bangala.
stops.quote: Finally, on 17 August at Banalya, 90 miles upstream from Yambuya, Stanley found Bonny, the sole European left in charge of the column, along with a handful of starving carriers.

stops.text: After returning to Fort Bodo, the expedition left Kavalli's on 10 April, passed Lake Edward and Lake George and reached Mackay's mission at Usambiro on 28 August. Commissioner Wissmann met it on 4 December and escorted it into Bagamoyo.
stops.quote: were met by commissioner Wissmann on 4 December and escorted into Bagamoyo.

notes: Order of stops: every stop's place in the order is stated in the article's own sentences (see report). Years are given only where the same sentence or the Emin Pasha article names them (Cairo 1887; April 1888); other stops keep the article's day and month with year null. The article contradicts itself on the meeting: Jephson met Emin at Mswa on 29 April 1888 and Emin met Stanley 'on the 29th', yet Emin's letter reached Stanley on 18 April; the Emin Pasha article says only 'April 1888', so the stop uses that. The meeting place is 'the south end of the lake' only; Lake Albert is used for its point. Left out: Suez, Aden, Bolobo, Bangala Station, Stanley Falls, Ugarrowwa's, Ipoto, Mswa, Dufile, Kavalli's (no dependable article title or a mere passing mention). 'by' of the first stop (London to Cairo) is not stated; sea assumed. Unsure wp titles: Ibwiri, Banalia, Usambiro, Banana (Democratic Republic of the Congo). EDITOR: Fort Bodo (Ibwiri) and Usambiro have no Wikipedia article, so no point: they are told in the texts of Lake Albert, Banalya and Bagamoyo. The two stops at Lake Albert are one; its point is the lake's, not its south end. Banalya takes the point of Banalia Territory, whose seat it is.
